title: Bildad Describes the Fate of the Wicked
overview: Job's friend Bildad answers Job's complaints with a grim poem about how wicked people are always destroyed, and he clearly means it as a picture of Job.

parts.label: Bildad loses patience (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Bildad is stung that Job seems to treat his friends as dull and stupid, and he accuses Job of tearing himself apart with his own anger. His question about moving rocks means roughly this: do you expect the settled order of the world to bend just for your sake?

parts.label: The light goes out (vv. 5-7)
parts.note: In that world a lamp usually burned in the tent all night, and a fire may also have signalled welcome to travelers, so a dark tent meant a household that was finished. Bildad says the wicked person's life and success will go dark like that, and his own plans will trip him up.

parts.label: Caught in every trap (vv. 8-10)
parts.note: Bildad piles up hunting words, a net, a snare, a noose, a hidden trap, to say the wicked walk into ruin by their own steps. The point is that there is no escape.

parts.label: Terror, disease and death (vv. 11-14)
parts.note: Fear chases him, and a disease pictured as death's eldest child, probably meaning the deadliest illness death can bring, eats away his body. "The king of terrors" pictures death itself as a ruler who leads him away.

parts.label: Nothing left behind (vv. 15-19)
parts.note: Burning sulfur falls on his home, perhaps recalling the fire that struck Job's flocks (Job 1:16) or the fate of Sodom, and his family line dries up like a dead tree until no one remembers his name. This closely matches what Job has already lost, his children, his property and his health, so Bildad's words are aimed straight at him.

parts.label: Everyone is horrified (vv. 20-21)
parts.note: People from west to east, meaning everyone, are shocked at his end. Bildad sums up that this is what happens to anyone who does not know God, though the book later says the friends spoke wrongly about God (Job 42:7).

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Bildad's picture of the wicked is a true principle that he wrongly applies to Job, or a view of suffering that the book of Job as a whole sets out to reject.
think: When someone is suffering badly, what makes it tempting to look for a reason they brought it on themselves?
